title: What Causes Poor Indoor Air Quality in Offices?
h1: What Causes Poor Indoor Air Quality in Offices?
description: Stuffy offices usually come down to low ventilation, dirty HVAC parts, moisture and indoor pollutants. Learn the common causes and how owners fix them.
quick_answer: Poor office air quality usually comes from too little fresh outdoor air, dirty filters, coils and ducts, moisture problems and pollutants released inside, like chemicals from furniture, cleaning products and printers. Crowded rooms raise carbon dioxide, and outside sources such as traffic or wildfire smoke can be pulled in through air intakes.
body:
When people say an office feels stuffy, gives them headaches or smells odd, the HVAC system is usually part of the story. Commercial buildings depend on mechanical ventilation, and small maintenance gaps can affect everyone who works there. Here are the causes we see most often in offices across San Diego and Orange County.

Is the office getting enough fresh air?

Commercial HVAC systems are designed to bring in a set amount of outdoor air and mix it with return air. Over time, that can drift:

  • Outdoor air dampers stuck closed or set too low to save energy
  • Economizer controls that have failed or been disabled
  • Rooftop units with clogged intake screens
  • Office layouts changed with new walls, but no changes to supply and return air

When fresh air drops, carbon dioxide and other pollutants build up, especially in conference rooms and busy areas. People often notice it as afternoon drowsiness or a stale feeling.

How do dirty HVAC parts affect office air?

Filters, coils and drain pans need regular service. When they're neglected:

  • Loaded filters let dust bypass the system or restrict airflow
  • Dirty evaporator coils collect dust and can grow biological slime
  • Standing water in drain pans can produce musty odors
  • Ductwork accumulates dust that blows out of diffusers, often visible as dark streaks on ceiling tiles

A scheduled maintenance plan keeps these from building up. Our commercial HVAC services cover rooftop units, ductwork and dryer vents for businesses.

What pollutants come from inside the office?

Many office materials release chemicals called volatile organic compounds, or VOCs:

  • New carpet, furniture, paint and adhesives
  • Cleaning products and air fresheners
  • Printers and copiers
  • Personal care products and food in break rooms

Renovation dust is another big one. Construction in an occupied building can send fine dust through the return air unless the area is sealed off and the system is protected.

Can moisture and mold be a factor?

Yes. Roof leaks, plumbing leaks, clogged condensate lines and wet ceiling tiles can all lead to mold growth. Buildings near the coast deal with more humid air, which gives moisture problems less chance to dry out. A musty smell, stained tiles or recurring allergy complaints from one area are worth investigating.

What outside sources get pulled indoors?

Outdoor air is only as clean as the area around the intake. Watch for:

  • Air intakes near loading docks, parking garages or busy streets
  • Smoking areas close to doors or intakes
  • Wildfire smoke and dust during Santa Ana wind events
  • Exhaust from kitchen hoods or plumbing vents near intakes on the roof

During smoke events, higher-rated filters, adjusted outdoor air settings and portable purifiers in key rooms can help, depending on what the equipment allows.

What signs point to an air quality problem?

Air problems rarely announce themselves directly. Facility managers usually hear about them as complaints:

  • Several people in the same area reporting headaches, dry eyes or fatigue
  • Rooms that feel stuffy by midafternoon, especially conference rooms
  • Odors that come and go when the system cycles
  • Dust on desks and around diffusers soon after cleaning
  • Hot and cold spots that suggest airflow isn't balanced

Write down where and when complaints happen. A pattern tied to one zone, one rooftop unit or one time of day makes the cause much easier to track down.

How can building owners improve office air quality?

  1. Keep a maintenance schedule. Regular filter changes, coil cleaning and drain service are the foundation.
  2. Check ventilation settings. Have dampers, economizers and controls verified so the building gets the outdoor air it was designed for.
  3. Upgrade filtration. Many units can use higher-rated filters if airflow allows.
  4. Clean the ducts when needed. Visible dust at diffusers, debris or post-construction contamination are good reasons.
  5. Control moisture. Fix leaks quickly and replace wet ceiling tiles.
  6. Monitor. Simple carbon dioxide and particle monitors help show whether changes are working.

For persistent complaints, an indoor air quality check can narrow down the cause. Learn more on our indoor air quality page.
faqs: It's a term for symptoms like headaches, fatigue, and eye or throat irritation that people feel in a building and that ease after they leave. Poor ventilation and indoor pollutants are common contributors.
How often should office HVAC filters be changed?
It depends on the equipment, filter type and how dusty the area is. Many commercial systems are checked monthly or quarterly as part of a maintenance plan, with changes made when filters load up.
Does high carbon dioxide mean the air is unsafe?

Normal office carbon dioxide levels aren't toxic, but rising levels show that ventilation isn't keeping up with the number of people. That often comes with stuffiness and other pollutants building up.
Should office air ducts be cleaned?
Duct cleaning makes sense when there's visible dust or debris, contamination after construction, pest activity or mold. An inspection can show whether it's needed.
